newsitem.title: EGYPT: U.S. denies seeking Sudan government change.
newsitem.headline: U.S. denies seeking Sudan government change.

text.p: The United States denied on Monday it was seeking a change in the Sudan government by providing military aid to the African country's neighbours.
The Chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff Army General John Shalikashvili was speaking to reporters after a meeting with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak in a Cairo palace.
Asked for his views on allegations that the United States might have an interest in changing Sudan's government by giving military aid to its neighbours, Shalikashvili said:
"First of all we did not discuss that particular issue. I do not feel that it is appropriate for me to comment on it other than to say that it simply is not a fact. Those are baseless allegations."
The United States has put Sudan on its list of countries that sponsor political violence.

But it denied in November it was seeking to overthrow the Sudan government, after reports published in the Washington Post newspaper said the U.S. would send nearly $20 million in surplus military equipment to Ethiopia, Uganda and Eritrea, which are on bad terms with Khartoum's Islamist rulers.
The Post had said congressional sources doubted the aid would be kept from rebel forces fighting Sudan's rulers.
Sudan responded to the report by saying it would collect $20 million to help the army against what it said were U.S. attempts to overthrow the government.
Shalikashvili, who arrived in Cairo on Saturday at the start of a Middle East trip, said he discussed the "general situation here in the region" during his talks in Egypt.
He said Egypt-U.S. military ties were "strong and very productive" and he also discussed arms, military manufacturing and joint training exercises with Egypt's defence minister.
Shalikashvili will return to Washington on January 10 after visiting Israel and Saudi Arabia, where the U.S. military is enforcing a no-fly zone over southern Iraq.
Egypt has had a role in discussions between Israel and Palestinians about handing over parts of the West Bank town of Hebron to Palestinian rule.

Asked about Israel and how the region could achieve stability, Shalikashvili said: "The discussions now on the peace process are in a very delicate state...(U.S.) President (Bill) Clinton is watching the situation very carefully and very closely. We are all very hopeful that an agreement can be reached soon."
